analysis.title: Carsten's view of 2027
key_insights: ING's Global Head of Macro sees 2027 as potentially a surprisingly benign year for the global economy, provided politics, AI investment, stock markets and central banks fall into place at the right time.

The AI investment surge that has supported US growth and record equity highs is likely to ease somewhat in 2027. The spending is spreading into grids, power plants, infrastructure and firms only now adopting AI, so growth should be less spectacular but broader.
Falling energy prices are a prerequisite for the AI boom to end in a soft landing. If they fall, central banks may be able to stay on hold.

If energy prices stay high, central banks could be forced to raise rates more aggressively to contain inflation, with the risk of breaking something. The report says it might not be the tech sector that breaks.
Households and traditional industry now compete with AI and data centres for energy. Those traditional parts of the economy look more vulnerable to higher interest rates.
Even if energy prices fall as Middle East tensions ease, Europe keeps a structural disadvantage because its energy remains more expensive than for many competitors.

After the US midterms, the open question is whether Trump becomes a conventional lame duck or a less predictable angry duck. Early post-midterm statements pointed to a conciliatory tone, but the appointment of Stephen Miller as White House Chief of Staff points toward a more confrontational direction.

Europe risks following the US populist turn with a lag of years. Elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and possibly Germany carry risks of political fragmentation and more extreme economic policies.

The 2027 outlook uses a '3 calls' structure (base case, riskier call, bold call). The riskier and bold calls are not house view and are tail-risk scenarios. This note gives no figures or specific forecasts.
risk_factors: Energy prices staying high, forcing central banks to hike more aggressively.
Excessive monetary tightening, noting that some of history's biggest stock market crashes were preceded by sharp tightening.
Traditional parts of the economy are more vulnerable to higher rates as they compete with AI and data centres for energy.
Political fragmentation and more extreme economic policies in Europe.
A more confrontational Trump administration after the midterms.
A slowdown in AI investment weighing on US growth and equity markets.
geopolitical: US midterm elections have just taken place and Congress now has the power to push back against the president.
Stephen Miller appointed White House Chief of Staff, read as pointing to a more confrontational final two years for Trump.
Elections in France, Italy, Spain, Poland and possibly Germany in 2027 carry political fragmentation risk.
Recent riots in many European cities, tied to intergenerational conflict, cost of living and housing affordability.
Middle East tensions: energy prices could fall if they ease.
Battle for control of trade, technology and energy between major powers.

tension_points.bull_case: Falling energy prices let the AI boom end in a soft landing, and central banks can sit on the sidelines for the first time since the pandemic.
tension_points.bear_case: High energy prices force central banks to raise rates more aggressively to contain inflation from an AI-fuelled boom, risking damage to traditional parts of the economy and financial markets.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Energy prices remaining high rather than falling.

theme_stances.key_argument: 2027 macro environment could prove more benign than many fear if politics, AI investment, markets and central banks align in timing.
theme_stances.evidence: next year's macro environment could prove more benign than many fear

theme_stances.key_argument: If energy prices stay high, central banks may have to tighten harder and something could break, possibly outside tech.
theme_stances.evidence: Central banks could become the circuit breaker
